items.title: Distance from the climatic niche optimum explains climate‐change‐driven dynamics in Mediterranean shrublands
items.abstract: Understanding vegetation responses to climatic variability is essential for anticipating future trajectories and informing management and conservation. Climatic niche metrics can improve climatic impact assessments by accounting for species‐specific climatic requirements. We analysed vegetation responses to gradual changes in climatic conditions in the monte blanco shrubland of Doñana National Park (SW Spain), one of Europe's most biodiverse protected areas. Specifically, we assessed vegetation dynamics over a 15‐year period (2007–2022) following a drought‐induced canopy loss event. We used species' climatic niche centroids as a proxy for their climatic optima and quantified their distance to observed climatic conditions as an indicator of climatic disequilibrium. We then examined temporal trends in centroid distance at community and species levels and tested their association with changes in shrub cover and community composition. Climatic conditions progressively shifted toward greater aridity during the study period, increasing centroid distance for all species but at different rates. Moreover, species‐specific rates of increase in centroid distance were associated with changes in shrub cover, although these changes mainly involved two of the ten species studied. The former dominant Halimium halimifolium, initially with the lowest centroid distance but experiencing the largest increase through time, declined in cover. By contrast, Salvia rosmarinus , which showed the highest initial centroid distance but a smaller increase, expanded. Consequently, community composition shifted, with H. halimifolium largely replaced by S. rosmarinus , while other species remained relatively stable. Although total shrub cover increased over the study period, it did not recover pre‐drought levels. Synthesis and applications . Assessing temporal changes in climatic disequilibrium can improve our understanding of vegetation dynamics under climate change. In Doñana shrublands, this approach helped explain contrasting species responses to gradual aridification, suggesting partial adaptation of community composition to emerging climatic conditions without overall cover loss. These assessments can inform conservation and adaptation planning by identifying potentially vulnerable taxa where vegetation data are limited and indicating whether community reorganization reflects adaptation to changing climatic conditions. By reliying on publicly available data, this approach offers a practical tool for assessing climatic impacts and management across terrestrial ecosystems worldwide.

items.title: Partitioning the variance of species–area relation into sampling‐ versus scale‐dependent components
items.abstract: The species–area relation (SAR) has been extensively studied over the past century, yet the sources of variation around an estimated SAR curve remain poorly understood. Here, we show that the sampling variance of the SAR can be decomposed into two additive components: 1) conditional variance, assuming that regional richness is fixed and represents uncertainty associated with local sampling; and 2) an additional component attributable to uncertainty in regional species richness, including uncertainty arising from rare species that remain undetected in the regional sample. We establish this decomposition mathematically and evaluate its behavior through numerical simulations. On this basis, empirical SAR observations can be classified as falling within the conditional confidence interval (CI), within the gap between the conditional and unconditional CIs, or outside the unconditional CI. The last outcome indicates variation not accounted for by the two sampling‐dependent components and may reflect scale‐dependent ecological processes or other sources of unexplained variation. Empirical applications showed that the relative contributions of local sampling uncertainty, regional richness uncertainty, and variation beyond these sampling‐dependent components differed among datasets, spatial scales, and sampling designs. For spatially explicit sampling of a tropical forest plot stem‐mapping dataset, observations were generally consistent with local sampling uncertainty when small sampling grains were freely distributed across space. In contrast, observations from a single contiguous sampling area more frequently fell outside the unconditional CI, a pattern that may reflect spatially structured ecological processes not represented by the sampling‐variance components. For nested sampling of amphibian diversity on the Chengdu Plain in SW China, both local sampling uncertainty and variation beyond the unconditional CI were frequently observed, whereas uncertainty in regional richness became more prominent when the local sampling area fraction exceeded 0.6. The resulting classifications also varied with the order of nested sampling: for the amphibian dataset, the large‐to‐small scheme accumulated species richness more slowly than the small‐to‐large scheme did. In conclusion, we develop a novel and readily applicable hierarchical variance‐partitioning framework to distinguish variation attributable to local sampling, uncertainty in regional richness, and variation not explained by these sampling‐dependent components along SAR curves.

items.title: Large‐Scale Biogeographic Structuring of Pacific Abyssal Communities Revealed by eDNA Metabarcoding
items.abstract: Aim At depths between 3000 and 6000 m, abyssal plains comprise over half of Earth's surface yet remain among the least biologically characterised ocean regions, particularly in the central Pacific where remoteness has constrained understanding of biodiversity and biogeography. Here, we apply environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding across abyssal sites between Mexico, Hawai‘i and Tahitī spanning > 5700 km to investigate broad‐scale biogeographic structuring and characterise biodiversity patterns. Location Abyssal Pacific Ocean. Methods We applied two fish‐targeted assays (MiFish‐U and 16S Fish) and one broad metazoan assay (COI Leray) to 252 eDNA samples collected from 4289 to 5666 m using near‐bottom Niskin water sampling and passive substrates (filter papers and polyurethane foam). Results Across the transects, 256 species spanning 123 families and 14 metazoan phyla were identified. Community composition differed between transects and among sites, revealing spatial structuring at regional and local scales. These patterns were supported by significant distance‐decay relationships, although strength varied among assays. Community differences were overwhelmingly driven by taxonomic turnover rather than nestedness, indicating abyssal assemblages comprise distinct regional communities rather than nested subsets of a cosmopolitan fauna. This structuring was associated with geographic position and environmental gradients, including depth and bottom‐water properties, indicating that community composition is structured by basin‐scale gradients and local habitat variation across the sampled transects. Sampling method influenced biodiversity detection but did not override spatial patterns, with active and passive approaches capturing complementary components of the community. Main Conclusions Across more than 5700 km of the Pacific abyssal plain, biodiversity was structured across multiple spatial scales rather than being homogeneous. eDNA resolves both basin‐scale biogeographic patterns and site‐level ecological variation, revealing how biodiversity is organised across a vast and under‐characterised biome. By capturing biodiversity largely inaccessible to conventional sampling, eDNA provides a powerful approach for resolving the distribution and organisation of life in Earth's largest biome.

items.title: Climatic Niche‐Based Identification of In‐Situ Climate Refugia to Support China's Conservation Planning Toward the 30 × 30 Target
items.abstract: Aim Climate change increasingly threatens biodiversity by altering habitat conditions and undermining the long‐term effectiveness of protected area (PA) networks. In situ climate refugia—locations that retain relatively stable climatic conditions—are essential for supporting species persistence under future climate scenarios and for meeting global conservation targets such as “30 × 30.” This study aims to identify in situ climate refugia across China using a climatic niche–based framework and to assess the degree to which these refugia are represented within the existing PA network. Location Mainland China. Time Period Baseline (1970–2000) and future projections for 2081–2100 under SSP2‐4.5 and SSP5‐8.5 scenarios Major Taxa Studied 282 endangered terrestrial vertebrates, including 68 mammals, 153 amphibians, 35 reptiles, and 26 non‐migratory birds. Methods We developed a climatic niche–based framework that integrates species‐specific climatic tolerances, climate change intensity, and habitat suitability to identify potential climate refugia at a national scale. Unlike traditional approaches reliant on broad, species‐neutral climate stability thresholds, our method uses species‐specific climatic niche widths (CNWs) to derive ecologically grounded climatic tolerance thresholds, enabling more species‐informed identification of refugial areas. Results Approximately 23% of mainland China's land area was classified as high‐potential climate refugia, concentrated mainly in the subtropical evergreen broadleaf forest and tropical monsoon rainforest. However, only 15% of these areas currently fall within PAs. Incorporating high‐potential refugia alone could increase national PA coverage from 19% to 38%, while adding medium‐potential refugia could raise overall protection to 56%. Main Conclusions Species‐specific CNWs provide a realistic and ecologically informed basis for delimiting refugia under climate change. The pronounced mismatch between identified climate refugia and China's existing PA network highlights critical conservation gaps, especially within subtropical and tropical biomes. High‐ and medium‐potential refugia identify opportunities for further ecological assessment and protection planning toward the 30 × 30 target. The proposed framework is scalable and applicable to other regions seeking to incorporate climate‐adaptive principles into systematic conservation planning.

items.title: Ecological Processes Shape Species Diversity and Distributions in a Trans‐Tasman Velvet Worm Genus
items.abstract: Aim Studies on the geographic distributions of terrestrial invertebrates with Gondwanan legacies have often focused on historical biogeography without considering ecological processes. Here, we focus on species diversity and distributional patterns of the trans‐Tasman egg‐laying velvet worm genus Ooperipatellus and investigate how climatic niches and refugia have shaped the present‐day distributions seen in this group. Location Australia and Aotearoa New Zealand. Taxon Velvet worm genus Ooperipatellus (Onychophora, Peripatopsidae). Methods We combined ultraconserved element (UCE) data and species delimitation with divergence dating and climatic niche analyses to explore the role of climate change in shaping present‐day species diversity and distributions. Results Our genomic data provide evidence for six putative new species of Ooperipatellus in Aotearoa New Zealand. We also show that the two main Ooperipatellus clades, AUS and NZ, occupy largely different environmental conditions, partly because the NZ niche lies in climates absent from Australia today. Occupied environmental space is more partitioned among Australian species than among New Zealand species, which show greater overlap. This is in contrast to geographic range overlap, which appears greater in Tasmania than in New Zealand. Niche models indicate that suitable environment for Ooperipatellus on the mainland of Australia has contracted since the Last Glacial Maximum, with species today currently occupying climate refugia. This analysis also reveals the presence of historical refugia in northwestern Tasmania which we hypothesize may have contributed to the east–west biodiversity patterns documented on the island. Most divergences among NZ Ooperipatellus species postdate the onset of the uplift of Kā Tiritiri o te Moana (the Southern Alps). One such divergence highlights a phylogeographic relationship across the southern Alpine Fault, this pattern is also replicated in other, distantly related taxa. Main Conclusions Our exploration of biogeographic patterns in this genus of rare saproxylic invertebrates underscores the dynamic interplay of organism, climate and geography in shaping taxon distributions and generating and maintaining diversity. The two main Ooperipatellus clades differ in the environmental conditions they occupy and in how they partition environmental and geographic space. The putative role of climatic refugia in shaping the distributions of these animals highlights the evolutionary complexity and contemporary vulnerability of these species.

items.title: Climate Change and Habitat Loss Threaten Taxonomic and Functional Diversity of Endemic Primates in South America
items.abstract: Aim To assess impacts of climate change and forest cover on taxonomic and functional diversity of endemic and threatened primates in South America. Location South America. Taxon Endemic and threatened primates. Methods We modelled climatic suitability for 68 taxa using consensus species distribution models for a baseline period (1981–2010) and two future periods (2041–2070; 2071–2100), under an intermediate (SSP3‐7.0) and a high‐end (SSP5‐8.5) emission scenario. The projections incorporated dispersal constraints and were combined with forest cover scenarios. Taxonomic diversity was estimated as species richness, whereas functional diversity was quantified as mean pairwise distance (MPD), which represents the average functional dissimilarity among co‐occurring taxa based on body mass, activity pattern, habitat, and trophic guild, at a 5 km resolution. The spatial congruence between taxonomic and functional diversity was assessed using geographically weighted correlation and generalized additive models. Results Most taxa showed a significant contraction of suitable range, especially under the most severe scenario (SSP5‐8.5 in 2071–2100), when more than half were projected to lose > 50% of their distribution. Areas of higher taxonomic and functional diversity were projected to contract in the Amazon and the Atlantic Forest, persisting mainly in the southwestern Amazon and the Magdalena River region. Under this scenario, taxa projected to lose more than 50% of their suitable area represented 23.3% of the summed functional distinctiveness of the 178‐taxon primate pool. The congruence between taxonomic and functional diversity increases in future projections, reflecting a concentration of species and functions in climatically more stable areas. Main Conclusions Climate change associated with forest loss may promote taxonomic erosion and functional simplification of primate communities. The projected increase in congruence may reflect environmental filtering and concentration in potential refugia, rather than ecological stability. Conservation strategies should incorporate functional metrics and prioritize areas that maintain functionally distinct taxa, as well as overall diversity.

items.title: Coupled MaxEnt-InVEST modelling identifies habitat suitability, quality and conservation gaps of Garrulax maximus
items.abstract: Introduction Habitat degradation and conservation gaps severely threaten China's endemic montane birds, yet few studies have integrated habitat suitability with quality assessment. Methods Using the nationally protected Giant Laughingthrush (Garrulax maximus) across five provinces in western China and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, we coupled optimized MaxEnt, InVEST, and GIS approaches to quantify potential distribution, habitat quality, conservation gaps, and environmental drivers. ResultsThe MaxEnt model performed robustly (mean AUC = 0.946). Climate dominated distribution (69.3% cumulative contribution), with annual precipitation (bio12, 35.7%) as the core limiting factor. The species occupied a cold-humid niche: annual precipitation 631.60–794.65 mm, driest-quarter temperature −7.12–2.75 °C, and elevation 2496.79–4012.78 m. High-suitability areas centered on the western Sichuan Basin rim, decreasing outward. Notably, a spatial mismatch emerged between habitat quality and suitability: Yunnan held the largest high-quality habitat (17.28 × 104 km2) but limited priority conservation areas, whereas Sichuan, with less high-quality habitat (13.63 × 104 km2), contained the largest priority zones (6.95 × 104 km2), indicating complementarity rather than substitution. Conservation gaps were extensive (54.26%–75.98%), mainly along reserve boundaries and buffers, revealing structural deficiencies from overemphasizing core zones while neglecting corridors. DiscussionThese findings underscore the urgency of reassessing and expanding protected area networks to cover priority zones. Our integrated framework offers a scientific reference for conserving the Giant Laughingthrush and managing montane birds within the Hengduan Mountains biodiversity hotspot, with implications for broader conservation planning in ecologically sensitive regions.

items.title: Climate change drives northward range shifts in invasive forest pests and pathogens
items.abstract: Invasive tree pests and pathogens are increasingly threatening forests worldwide. Understanding how a warming climate and changing precipitation patterns will affect the future distribution ranges of these pathogenic species requires systematic analysis across a variety of host trees and pathogenic species. We analysed 31 major tree pests and pathogens that have caused widespread and extensive damage globally, predicting their current and future distribution under various climate change scenarios using species distribution modelling. Our results showed that tree pests and pathogens will consistently shift northward, threatening northern temperate and boreal forests between the years 2041 and 2080. On the other hand, some warmer regions, including southern Europe, were expected to experience fewer pest and pathogen outbreaks in the future. Annual mean temperature, mean temperature of the warmest quarter, precipitation of the warmest quarter, and precipitation of the driest month contributed to the species distribution models, indicating that warming temperatures and moderate precipitation may promote the survival, reproduction, and spread of the pathogenic agents. Our research highlights the need for enhanced monitoring, early pest and pathogen detection, stricter biosecurity measures, and improved silvicultural strategies in temperate and boreal forests in the northern hemisphere. Moreover, forest assessments, including those focused on carbon budgets, biodiversity, and ecosystem services, should account for the effects of tree pests and pathogen outbreaks, as they may drastically alter future functioning of forests globally.

items.title: Assessing Strategies to Optimize Participatory Science Data in Species Distribution Models
items.abstract: Aims Data from participatory science projects are widely used to understand species distributions. However, participatory science data often contain biases that can obscure real patterns. We address two sources of sampling bias: location uncertainty of individual records and spatially heterogeneous sampling effort. A variety of data processing and modelling strategies have been used to address these biases, without consensus on their relative effectiveness. We test several strategies using data from iNaturalist, a large repository of participatory science data. Location Twenty‐four amphibian ranges of varying sizes and locations within the continental United States. Method We fit species distribution models with iNaturalist data for 24 amphibian species to compare the effectiveness of strategies intended to improve distribution estimates. We examined three categories of strategies: (1) filtering out records with high location uncertainty, (2) thinning to reduce heterogeneous effort, and (3) observation models that account for heterogeneous effort without removing data. We evaluated the predictive accuracy of each approach using validation data from systematic surveys with constant effort and known locations. Results The strategies we tested generally had little effect on predictive accuracy as measured by AUC, with no consistent pattern across species. Instead, we found that the minimal change in performance was influenced by the species‐specific search process, the distribution of records, and the resolution of the analysis. Main Conclusion None of the strategies we tested consistently improve model performance, but our results provide a foundation for a species‐ and analysis‐specific approach. Further improvement in model performance may require additional information or novel methods.

items.title: Protected Areas Reduce Heat Exposure in Squamates Globally
items.abstract: Protected areas (PAs) are central to biodiversity conservation, yet their capacity to buffer species from climate‐driven heat exposure, that is, the duration and frequency of exposure to temperatures exceeding species' critical thermal limits, remains poorly quantified at global scales. Here, we assessed whether squamate reptiles inside PAs experience lower heat exposure than conspecifics in unprotected, human‐modified landscapes, and how this buffering effect varies across latitudes, biomes, and evolutionary lineages. Using biophysical modelling of operative temperatures across 248 species, we show that PAs consistently reduced both annual hours above critical thermal maximum (CT max ) and the frequency of critical days under current and future climatic scenarios (+2°C and + 4°C). We found that under current climate, protected sites had 51 fewer hours above CT max and 3.5 fewer critical days than unprotected sites, and the proportional reduction persisted under +2°C and + 4°C warming scenarios. The buffering effect was most pronounced at low latitudes and tropical biomes, where species already operate close to their thermal limits. Deserts and xeric shrublands, together with tropical grasslands and savannas, emerged as biomes with elevated heat exposure, reinforcing growing concern for arid‐zone reptiles under climate change. Substantial phylogenetic signal in heat exposure indicated that evolutionary history shapes thermal vulnerability beyond geography and biome alone, with the magnitude of PA buffering varying considerably across squamate lineages. Our findings demonstrate that PAs can provide refugia from heat exposure, and that their conservation value under climate change depends on the retention of structurally complex habitats and thermally heterogeneous microhabitats.

items.title: Climate‐driven compositional shifts across a temperate–subtropical island ecotone
items.abstract: Climate change is expected to drive substantial shifts in species distributions, yet ecological responses are often delayed under disequilibrium dynamics, limiting the effectiveness of range‐based indicators for detecting ongoing change. Compositional approaches have been proposed as an alternative; however, conventional comparisons based on gradient shape or pointwise differences may fail to detect change when the overall gradient structure is conserved, because small and spatially heterogeneous differences cancel out across the gradient. Here, we address this limitation by presenting a direction‐sensitive analytical framework that integrates signed differences along environmental gradients. Using a comprehensive dataset of island floras across a temperate–subtropical transition in South Korea, we quantify temporal changes in the relative representation of warm‐temperate and subtropical plant (WTSP) assemblages. By emphasizing proportional changes along latitudinal gradients, we detect directional redistribution within communities even in the absence of pronounced changes in gradient shape. Our results reveal patterns consistent with northward redistribution of WTSP composition across survey periods, despite minimal changes in overall gradient form, indicating that community‐level redistribution can occur prior to detectable range shifts or richness changes. These findings highlight the sensitivity of cumulative, direction‐sensitive compositional metrics for detecting early ecological responses to climate warming. More broadly, this study provides a generalizable framework for detecting compositional redistribution through cumulative inference, even when conventional approaches may have limited sensitivity under some conditions, and for identifying early signals of climate‐driven change across gradient‐structured ecological systems. Transitional systems may therefore serve as particularly sensitive contexts for detecting incipient biogeographical change under ongoing warming.

items.title: Assessing the accuracy and stability of variable importance in species distribution modelling algorithms through sample perturbations
items.abstract: Variable importance derived from species distribution modelling (SDM) is widely used to identify key environmental drivers of species distributions. However, the reliability of these inferences has rarely been systematically evaluated, particularly with respect to their sensitivity to individual occurrences. Here, we used virtual species and developed a sample perturbations diagnostic framework, in which each occurrence was systematically removed (leave‐one‐out) to assess how small changes in the input data affect variable importance inference. Using this framework, we evaluated and compared ten SDM algorithms across multiple scenarios. We constructed a set of evaluation metrics to quantify both the accuracy of driver identification and the stability of permutation importance estimates, defined as their variability under sample perturbations. We further investigated the sample level mechanisms underlying instability. Our results showed that random forest (RF), gradient boosting machine (GBM), and maximum entropy (Maxent) achieved the best overall performance. RF exhibited the relatively high inferential accuracy and stability, but showed limited ability to differentiate the relative importance of environmental variables. GBM and Maxent achieved slightly lower accuracy than RF, but were more stable and effective for distinguishing the relative contributions of different variables. Instead, several algorithms displayed relatively high accuracy but were sensitive to sample perturbations. Scenario analyses indicated that stability generally increased under conditions of high sample sizes, low geographical sampling bias, and moderate prevalence. Highly influential occurrences were not necessarily associated with extreme environmental conditions. Removal experiments further demonstrated that variable importance inference in several algorithms was sensitive to a relatively small subset of occurrences, highlighting the disproportionate contribution of these occurrences. Overall, this study provides a sample level diagnostic framework for evaluating the reliability of variable importance in SDM, offering practical guidance for improving the interpretability of environmental driver inference in ecological research and conservation applications.

items.title: Hunters in Danger: Evolutionary Diversity and Conservation Priorities in Carnivore Species of the American Continent
items.abstract: Aim Many mammals of the order Carnivora are key ecosystem predators. In the American continent, they have a complex biogeographical history, shaped by processes of colonization and adaptive radiation that have generated a high diversity of lineages. However, under the global biodiversity crisis, this group faces increasing extinction risk, and conservation efforts have focused mainly on species richness while neglecting evolutionary relationships. We aimed to assess the distribution of evolutionary diversity in carnivores of the American continent and its relationship with biological and geographical variables to recognize species and areas with unique evolutionary value. Location American continent. Methods We evaluated 104 carnivore species of the Americas. Using data from public literature, we calculated Evolutionary Distinctiveness (ED), Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered (EDGE; EDGE2), and Biogeographically weighted Evolutionary Distinctiveness (BED) metrics. In addition, we explored the relationship between evolutionary scores with body size, altitudinal and latitudinal distribution of species, and mapped spatial patterns of richness and evolutionary metrics to identify priority areas for conservation. Results The evolutionary diversity of carnivores was unevenly distributed across regions and taxonomic groups. In terrestrial species, all evolutionary scores decreased with altitude, and only ED followed a unimodal pattern with latitude, concentrating in the tropical belt; in marine species, ED clustered in the temperate zones of the Northern Hemisphere. A positive relationship was detected between body size and ED in marine species, and a negative relationship was observed with BED in terrestrial species and across all carnivores. Spatial patterns of richness were consistent with those of ED, EDGE and EDGE2 scores, but differed from those obtained with BED scores. Main Conclusion Our findings demonstrate the importance of incorporating evolutionary metrics into the prioritization of American carnivores as a means to safeguard their evolutionary history and to optimize conservation planning and resource allocation from a comprehensive perspective.

items.title: Metabolic ecology and habitat stability explain the disproportionately high species richness in standing waters
items.abstract: The metabolic theory of ecology (MTE) conceptualizes that temperature is the primary driver of species richness, a pattern well supported in terrestrial taxa but less certain for freshwater organisms. Limited global‐scale evidence and frequent violations of MTE's assumptions, particularly regarding the stationarity of body size and abundance, further undermine its applicability. In freshwater systems, body size and abundance are tightly linked to dispersal and range size, which differ markedly between running‐water (lotic) and standing‐water (lentic) species, as proposed by the Habitat‐Stability–Dispersal Hypothesis (HSDH). Adaptations to habitat stability may therefore generate distinct biogeographical patterns of traits and modify richness–temperature relationships predicted by MTE. Utilizing comprehensive global functional, phylogenetic, and distributional data on dragonfly and damselfly species (83%) and habitat information (46%), we tested MTE predictions for lentic versus lotic species. Lotic species richness followed MTE expectations (slope: −0.469) more closely than lentic species richness (slope: −0.283). The proportion of lentic species in an assemblage was the strongest predictor of deviation in the species richness–temperature relationship ( R 2 = 38%). Assemblages dominated by lentic species clustered in climatically unstable regions and mainly included smaller‐bodied species with larger ranges. Phylogenetic comparative analysis shows a strong phylogenetic signal in habitat preference, with the most species‐rich and northerly distributed families comprising predominantly lentic species. Our findings suggest that adaptations to habitat stability facilitated the colonization and persistence of lentic species in harsh and fluctuating climates, both past and present, resulting in largely divergent species richness patterns of lentic and lotic odonates. Integrating HSDH‐related traits (body and range size) not only substantially improves the explanatory power of the MTE but also reveals a trait syndrome with broad implications for the biogeography and climate change responses of freshwater communities.

items.title: Human pressure, habitat heterogeneity and species traits jointly determine the level of dark diversity in coastal fish communities
items.abstract: Understanding how anthropogenic pressures and environmental gradients shape coastal fish communities is a central question in biogeography and marine conservation. Yet, the set of species expected to occur at a site given ecological conditions but being absent – the so‐called dark diversity – has received far less attention than observed species, even if they hold key information about local extirpations and conservation effectiveness. Quantifying dark diversity in the sea is particularly challenging because many species are rare, cryptobenthic or mobile, while sampling effort is rarely standardized. Here we combined 930 environmental DNA (eDNA) samples collected at 401 sites along 2000 km of the French Mediterranean coast with fine‐scale mapping of habitats, anthropogenic pressures and protection levels. Using a Bayesian model of dark diversity affinity (DDA) that explicitly controls for sampling effort, we decomposed the correlates of species absences into site characteristics and species traits, separating dispersal‐related from sensitivity‐related signals. At the site level, fishing effort, marine traffic, and artificial habitats were associated with greater DDA, so a deficit of species, whereas protected areas and diverse natural habitats were associated with lower DDA, increasing the likelihood of observing more complete fish communities. At the species level, demersal and predator species, together with those bearing their eggs (e.g. many elasmobranchs) compared to species with demersal or pelagic eggs, exhibited the highest DDA, suggesting local extirpations linked to a combination of limited dispersal and higher sensitivity to cumulative pressures. Beyond the creation of marine protected areas, preserving habitat heterogeneity and mitigating coastal pressures therefore emerge as essential levers to limit the local erosion of fish biodiversity. More broadly, coupling eDNA with a sampling‐effort‐corrected DDA framework offers a transferable benchmark to evaluate where, and for which species, conservation efforts are most needed.

items.title: ZonationR: An R interface to the Zonation software for reproducible spatial conservation prioritisation workflows
items.abstract: Systematic conservation planning provides a science‐based framework for defining conservation goals and supporting transparent spatial decision‐making under limited resources. Within this framework, spatial conservation prioritisation tools are widely used to identify areas of high biodiversity value by integrating information on species distributions, connectivity, costs, and other factors into spatially explicit recommendations. ‘Zonation' is one of the leading software tools in this field, producing hierarchical priority rankings of landscapes based on conservation value. However, its standard workflow typically relies on manual steps for data preparation, execution, and post‐processing, which can become inefficient and difficult to reproduce when multiple scenarios are analysed, limiting accessibility and broader uptake. We introduce ‘ZonationR', an R package that provides a streamlined interface to the ‘Zonation' software, enabling fully reproducible and automated spatial prioritisation workflows. The package integrates the entire analysis pipeline, encompassing input preparation, execution of ‘Zonation', and post‐processing, while supporting both single‐variant and multi‐variant workflows. ‘ZonationR' also provides tools to explore and interpret outputs, including priority maps, feature performance curves, cost summaries, feature representation metrics, and similarity assessments between prioritisation solutions. By linking directly to the original ‘Zonation' engine, the package enables users to benefit from ongoing methodological developments in ‘Zonation' and access its functionality through a transparent, script‐based workflow, thereby reducing technical barriers to running and understanding spatial prioritisation analyses. Beyond these advantages, its integration within the R environment supports iterative testing of conservation scenarios and more rigorous assessment of methodological decisions, while facilitating seamless connections with wider ecological workflows (e.g. species distribution modelling). As conservation planning increasingly relies on large, complex, multi‐source datasets and integrative approaches, such integration is essential for enabling robust, transparent, and reproducible decision‐making across spatial scales.

items.title: An Open Occurrence Dataset for European Subterranean Spiders
items.abstract: Motivation Spiders are common inhabitants of caves and other subterranean habitats, where they play key ecological roles as generalist predators and strongly influence local food webs. They have been instrumental as model organisms for testing various eco‐evolutionary hypotheses. Furthermore, strictly subterranean species exhibiting narrow ranges and high endemism are particularly significant for conservation planning and vulnerability assessments. Although high‐quality data are essential for research on and conservation of subterranean spiders, such information remains scarce, especially regarding distribution patterns. To help fill this gap, we screened the literature, unpublished records and open datasets to compile georeferenced occurrences of subterranean spiders across caves and other subterranean habitats throughout Europe. To illustrate one potential application of the compiled dataset, we also present a prediction of subterranean spider richness patterns across Europe using stacked species distribution models. Main Types of Variables Contained The European Subterranean Spider Dataset (ESSD) comprises 31,498 records of 637 subterranean‐dwelling spider species, covering a range of information including taxonomy, locality details (such as location name, country, geographic coordinates, type of subterranean habitat) and reference information for each record. All variables are coded using the Darwin Core Standard, ensuring interoperability with the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) and other biodiversity databases. Spatial Location and Grain The collected data are distributed across 42 countries within the European continent, with varying spatial uncertainty. Most coordinates of localities are taken at the cave entrance (uncertainty of ca. 10 m), or at the nearest hamlet when precise coordinates are not available (uncertainty of ca. 1 km). Time Period and Grain The data represent information made available between 1881 and 2026. Major Taxa and Level of Measurement 637 species (including morphospecies under description) of subterranean spiders across 28 families. These species span a gradient of ecological dependence on subterranean habitats, ranging from species still able to exploit surface habitats to obligate subterranean dwellers. Software Format The dataset is available in .csv format in Figshare data repository (available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.30696173 ) and in GBIF ( https://doi.org/10.15468/f4xjdb ).

items.title: Multi-scale modeling of continent-wide tracking data confirms the importance of landscape mosaics for the European wildcat
items.abstract: Context Land use change is a major threat to the persistence of wildlife in human-dominated landscapes, making the knowledge of the amount and spatial configuration of suitable habitat essential for conservation. The European wildcat ( Felis silvestris ) currently persists in fragmented populations and faces ever increasing human pressure. Objectives We modeled and mapped suitable wildcat habitats at the continental scale, to identify opportunities and constraints for its conservation. Methods We compiled a large telemetry dataset comprising 200 wildcats across Europe and developed multi-scale habitat suitability models using Maxent. Habitat selection was analyzed at two hierarchical levels: home-range placement within the wider landscape and selection within the established home ranges. items.title: Contrasting climatic niche structure and projected suitability for Canada lynx and bobcat
items.abstract: We asked whether the Canada lynx ( Lynx canadensis ) and the bobcat ( Lynx rufus ) differ in the internal structure of their occupied climatic niches and whether any difference translates into contrasting mid-century projections across North America. We calibrated ensemble species distribution models on 6,721 Canada lynx and 9,030 bobcat records with six climatic predictors per species, compared them in environmental space, and projected suitability to 2041–2060 under two Shared Socioeconomic Pathways and three global climate models. The two species occupy divergent observed climatic niches, and the difference is not explained by the climates available to each. The models are dominated by different climatic axes rather than by different positions along a shared one: isothermality for the Canada lynx and cold-quarter potential evapotranspiration for the bobcat. They also differ in breadth, with three biomes holding almost all Canada lynx records, compared with seven for the bobcat. Both occupied niches extend to the edge of the climate available in North America, indicating that the broader climatic tolerance of either species may not be fully resolved from this continent alone. Projections diverge: suitable climate for the Canada lynx contracts, with losses concentrated in the alpine and subalpine homologs of its lowland core. Under the design we report, bobcat suitability expands into boreal biomes it currently barely occupies, and the area suitable for both more than doubles. Because projections depend on where background data are drawn, we repeated the workflow under four pseudo-absence schemes: the direction of change held for the Canada lynx but reversed for the bobcat, and we report both.

items.title: A Multidimensional Climatic Variability Hypothesis for Terrestrial Ectotherms
items.abstract: Aim The climatic variability hypothesis (CVH) predicts that ectotherms exposed to greater climatic variability evolve broader physiological tolerances, but its application to biogeography has been dominated by thermal traits. Here, the author argue that the CVH empirical testing warrants expansion beyond the thermal axis, using an existing mechanistic niche framework. Location Global. Major Taxa Studied Terrestrial ectotherms. Main Conclusions Evidence for thermal tolerance breadth is extensive and generally supports CVH predictions, but exceptions exist, largely driven by taxon‐specific responses and climatic extremes rather than variability. Evidence for hydric and energetic traits remains more limited but shows that water balance and metabolic traits vary across geographic gradients. These axes interact mechanistically, that is, dehydration can reduce thermal tolerance and performance, while water limitation can restrict the activity and foraging needed to meet metabolic costs. Testing these interactions at the distributional level requires models that capture them, yet current correlative species distribution models do not incorporate these interacting constraints. Mechanistic and hybrid models provide a way for integrating physiological data into forecasts of range limits and vulnerability to climate change. The major empirical gap is the scarcity of datasets that measure thermal, hydric and energetic traits simultaneously in the same groups of organisms across environmental gradients. A multidimensional CVH provides a testable framework for improving mechanistic understanding and prediction of terrestrial ectotherm responses to global change.

items.title: Two decades of Landsat images reveal spatial and temporal dynamics of invasion and improve species distribution models
items.abstract: Developing accurate and cost‐effective methods to detect and predict the spread of invasive species remains an ongoing challenge. Species distribution models (SDMs) are widely used to predict invasion under current and future climates and inform management strategies. However, occurrence datasets are often spatially and temporally biased due to unstructured and opportunistic data collection. Remote sensing of individual species over broad spatial and temporal scales has become increasingly feasible with the accumulation of satellite images and the development of convolutional neural networks. In this study, we used 21 years of archival Landsat satellite imagery (2000–2020) to train a land use/land cover (LULC) classification algorithm using a temporal convolutional neural network to predict occurrence of the invasive species, leafy spurge ( Euphorbia virgata ), across Minnesota. We validated our predictions with an independent dataset. First, we show that leafy spurge has expanded from 1067 km 2 in 2000–2002 to 7156 km 2 in 2018–2020, a 570% increase. Drought severity modulated the predicted area invaded and was associated with fluctuations over time. Second, we tracked changes in probability over time for individual pixels and showed that invasion has been concentrated in two largely disjunct regions that differ in climate. Third, our remotely sensed predicted occurrence dataset and community science dataset were closer to roadsides, suggesting that roadside disturbance facilitates invasion. Last, we showed that SDMs built using remotely sensed occurrences had higher discrimination, were less overfit, and performed better outside of urban areas. Overall, 21 years of archival satellite imagery showed rapid expansion in two geographically distinct regions, invasion associated with roads, and improved predictions of invasion.

items.title: Revealing the Widespread Bias of Extinction Risk in the Antarctic and the Southern Ocean
items.abstract: Accelerating environmental change in the Antarctic and Southern Ocean (ASO) necessitates robust extinction risk assessments to inform conservation priorities. Nevertheless, no systematic, region-wide baseline of extinction risk currently exists for tracking ASO biodiversity responses to ongoing change, a significant barrier to global biodiversity monitoring. Here, we conducted the first ASO-wide synthesis of current extinction risk knowledge for plants, animals and Fungi. This included examining biases in current assessments, the distribution of Threatened species and their associated threats. Using a data-inclusive workflow, we compiled 8908 assessments representing 4970 species, more than doubling the number of ASO species assessed compared with any single source. As expected, assessments were heavily biased towards vertebrates (58% assessed), while invertebrates, despite their ecological prevalence, were markedly underrepresented (6% assessed). Among vertebrates, mammals had the highest proportion of Threatened species (26%). Birds within the ASO were disproportionately Threatened (25%) compared to the global average (11%), with the greatest threat for ASO species being 'Biological Resource Use'. The sub-Antarctic Islands had the highest density of both Threatened species and assessment effort, whereas many Antarctic species remain unassessed. Additionally, Threatened species have the lowest protected area coverage of any conservation status. These pronounced assessment biases highlight the need for more balanced, representative and data-inclusive extinction risk assessments to be able to effectively detect conservation status change. This work represents an important step in ensuring ASO representation in global biodiversity monitoring frameworks, strengthening the capacity of these frameworks to detect, attribute and respond to future biodiversity changes.

items.title: Importance of scale in seascape habitat suitability modeling: Predicting species distributions in changing ecosystems
items.abstract: Habitat suitability models (HSMs) use landscape metrics to describe patterns in species distributions, quantify the success of habitat restoration, and model species responses to change. Within a particular level of organization, the spatial scale of effect at which habitat is integrated and incorporated into HSMs can influence model performance. However, scale optimization can be time consuming and requires high-quality data across spatial scales. As such, it is not widely applied in suitability models and is particularly rare in marine studies. In coastal and marine landscapes, or seascapes, rapidly changing seascape metrics and environmental contexts can disrupt known species-seascape relationships and complicate evaluations of habitat quality. Studying the effect of scale on species suitability models in these systems allows for greater predictive power and better understanding of the multiscale processes that drive species distributions. We use quantitative species abundance from a Louisiana Gulf coast estuary along with both drone and satellite-derived habitat data to model species-habitat relationships across a range of measurement scales. Using this approach, we identify optimal measurement scales for population-level HSMs for Penaeus setiferus (white shrimp) and Callinectes sapidus (blue crabs) and identify key species-habitat relationships. Within the range of scales considered (20-600-m radius), blue crab HSMs had the highest predictive power at 150 m. White shrimp showed high predictive power at both 120 m and 300 m in drone and satellite-based analyses, respectively. Our models show that white shrimp have a positive association with Avicennia germinans (black mangroves), a range-expanding foundation species rapidly encroaching onto the Spartina alterniflora marshes in Louisiana. This approach generates predictive HSMs for two key fisheries species on the Louisiana coast and helps define their relationship to ongoing changes in their habitat. Future seascape suitability studies should test across spatial scales to optimize the predictive power of their models.

items.title: Measuring the edges of species' geographic ranges
items.abstract: The fundamental unit of spatial ecology is a species range: the geographical area that it occupies. Species ranges are delineated by range edges (also known as boundaries or limits). Why range edges occur where they do and not elsewhere, and what makes them move, has been an active area of research since the 19th century. In the present day, range edge dynamics are an important metric of biodiversity's response to climate change, as species shift toward the poles to track their climatic niches. Yet there are many methods for measuring range edges and quantifying their displacement. Here I describe common methods for describing range edge positions and apply them to example data for a bird species and a fish species, using some of the most popular datasets in climate biogeography: the Audubon Society Christmas Bird Count and a National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration bottom trawl survey. I show that the choice of range edge metric influences where range edge positions are estimated to occur; whether they are estimated to be shifting over time; and the estimated rate of shift. The lack of standardized metrics for range edges has likely shaped statistics reported in synthesis studies that measured overall biodiversity responses to climate change and global rates of range shifts. Through simulation, I found that reliably detecting range edge shifts may require decades of data or more, suggesting that many global change studies in this field are underpowered. Pairing metrics to research questions, sharing raw data and code, and conducting power analyses before reporting statistically significant results will all help to minimize this issue. Going forward, the field of biogeography should confront the degree to which ad hoc methods have influenced our understanding of range edge dynamics and move towards standardized metrics.

items.title: DNA barcoding of more than one million insect specimens indicates that at least one third of California's insect biodiversity remains undiscovered
items.abstract: Insects are the most diverse terrestrial organisms, yet they are underrepresented in large‐scale conservation assessments. To address this gap, the California Insect Barcoding Initiative is developing a publicly accessible, statewide DNA‐barcode reference library for California insects to support scalable surveys, establish baseline biodiversity measurements, and generate potential distribution maps that inform conservation planning. Specimens are collected with a hybrid strategy that combines standardized Malaise trapping, to enable replicable sampling, and opportunistic collecting, to maximize taxonomic coverage. Using samples collected primarily from 2022–2024 at 72 longer‐term Malaise trap sites, coupled with collecting using varied methods at 454 additional locations across California, we have barcoded over one million specimens. Preliminary completeness analyses suggest that current sampling captures roughly 65–69% of the fauna, implying a conservative minimum of circa 61 000 insect species in California, as delimited by their DNA barcode sequence. Using all sequenced specimen records, we generated rule‐based spatial range interpolations constrained by ecoregion and vegetation type, and used these to infer spatial patterns in insect species richness across the state. We identify areas of both high and low potential species richness, with current peaks in the Southern California Mountains ecoregion and the Mojave Basin and Range ecoregion. Our species richness estimates and spatial patterns are explicitly provisional and are expected to evolve as sampling gaps are addressed. Finally, we make all sequence data, specimen images, and occurrence records publicly available via the Barcode of Life Datasystem. items.title: Behavioural Plasticity Is Associated With Climate Tracking in Birds
items.abstract: Aim To test whether behavioural plasticity is associated with birds' ability to track climate change and whether this relationship differs among spatial gradients and range positions. items.title: Decoupling environmental suitability from realized recruitment through ontogenetic environmental filtering in a long‐lived Mediterranean palm species
items.abstract: Long‐lived plants facing anthropogenic disturbance often exhibit recruitment failure despite persistent reproductive adults, generating extinction debt masked by longevity. However, whether adult presence reliably reflects environmental suitability for recruitment remains unclear. Here, we examine ontogenetic niche differentiation and its consequences for recruitment in Jubaea chilensis , an endangered long‐lived Mediterranean palm with an aging population. We assigned individuals within the largest known population to four ontogenetic stages and characterized their environmental niches using climatic, edaphic, topographic and vegetation variables. We then applied spatial and multivariate analyses, including random forest models to evaluate environmental segregation and identify predictors of seedling establishment. Saplings and adult differentiation reflected mainly topographic variables at landscape scale, whereas seedling establishment was primarily predicted by microhabitat conditions (vegetation cover heterogeneity, east‐facing slope orientation and soil texture). This pattern is consistent with niche reconfiguring throughout the life cycle, suggesting that adult occurrence and recruitment suitability respond to distinct environmental conditions. This divergence may be further intensified by ongoing climate change, particularly Mediterranean aridification, progressively narrowing the environmental space available for successful recruitment. Over one‐fifth of sampled individuals occupied high‐suitability sites without recruitment, suggesting that ontogenetic niche shifts are associated with a spatial decoupling between adult persistence and recruitment, consistent with demographic collapse independent of habitat degradation. This failure is likely mediated by insufficient effective seed dispersal, as the sole disperser Octodon degus preys on most seeds before dispersal. Conservation strategies based solely on adult distribution may therefore overestimate effective habitat and underestimate extinction risk in long‐lived species.

items.title: Intensification and Spatial Reorganization of Drought Risks for Global Rainfed Crops Under Climate Change
items.abstract: Rainfed agriculture covers roughly 80% of global cropland and supplies more than half of global food production, yet uncertainty in how meteorological drying propagates into root‐zone water deficits and crop losses impedes robust risk assessment. By 2070–2099, opposing‐direction SPEI–SSI change classes occupied 6.8%–28.4% of rainfed area across crops under SSP1‐2.6/default CO 2 and 26.6%–48.2% under SSP5‐8.5/default CO 2 . Comparison with fixed‐2015 CO 2 experiments (7.5%–27.6% and 21.7%–34.9%, respectively) indicates that elevated CO 2 substantially expanded the spatial footprint of this hydrometeorological decoupling. Historically, SSI‐defined drought affected 12–16 million ha year −1 and was associated with annual production losses of 5–12 Mt year −1 (1.6–2.0% year −1 ). Under default CO 2 , affected area increased to 14–21 million ha under SSP1‐2.6 and 19–27 million ha under SSP5‐8.5, with production losses of 6–12 and 9–12 Mt year −1 , respectively. Under default CO 2 , loss increases clustered in Central America, northeastern Brazil, western Europe and southern Africa; fixed‐2015 CO 2 broadened the area of robust grid‐cell loss increases. items.title: Incorporating reef condition into conservation planning to meet place‐based biodiversity outcomes under the Global Biodiversity Framework
items.abstract: To achieve Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) Target 3, the selection of protected areas must consider the condition of ecosystems at sites in addition to the GBF 30% area target. To address this uncertainty, we evaluated whether including ecosystem condition data changed conservation priorities when the objective was to protect reefs and implement Target 3. These differences in priority areas highlight the need to develop and use effective condition metrics for designing marine protected area systems for coral reefs globally. Making such data available and usable for managers and practitioners is a priority for coral reef conservation.

items.title: Plant species' distribution patterns, functional traits, and range shifts along an elevation gradient
items.abstract: Knowledge about species' distributions is essential for understanding biodiversity patterns and predicting responses to climate change. The shapes of species' density distributions reflect how their performance varies across their range – shaped by environment, biotic interactions, and dispersal. Because these distributions reflect emergent properties of populations, they may reveal deterministic processes underlying species' past and future ranges and range shifts. Yet, distribution shape parameters (DSPs) are rarely considered in this context, leaving their potential largely unexplored. We addressed this gap by asking: 1) How do DSPs vary and covary among mountain plant species? 2) How are DSPs related to plant functional traits? 3) Can DSPs and functional traits explain recent range shifts? We quantified DSPs for 283 species across 626 plots spanning a 2000‐m elevation gradient on the Calanda massif, Graubünden, Switzerland, extracted functional traits from the TRY database, and compared DSPs and functional traits to range‐shift rates from two complementary data sources. We found that observed range shapes formed a subset of all possible shapes, suggesting trade‐offs in the drivers of distribution shapes. For example, we found that species abundant at higher elevations had shorter upslope and longer downslope distribution tails, consistent with abiotic stress limitation. Range limits and optima were also correlated with functional traits and distribution skew with species' dispersal distance. Finally, both distribution shapes and functional traits correlated with ongoing range shifts – DSPs outperformed functional traits, but considering both provided greater explanatory power. Overall, our results demonstrate that DSPs offer promising directions for future research into the factors influencing range shifts and our ability to predict them. Specifically, the drivers of DSPs and the relevant temporal scales over which they operate should be explored, potentially providing further insights into species' range shifts.

items.title: Beta diversity analysis reveals high turnover in benthic assemblages between tropical coral and subtropical rocky reefs
items.abstract: Understanding species distributions and biodiversity patterns is an old challenge in ecology and biogeography. items.title: How do we know when invasive species control strategies work?
items.abstract: Controlling invasive species is costly and difficult but can have major ecological, economic, and health benefits. items.title: The interplay of landscape connectivity, composition and configuration in alien plant invasions across an ecological network
items.abstract: Context Biological invasions are deemed to be the second most important global driver of biodiversity loss showing strong interactions with the aftermaths of land use change and landscape fragmentation. The role of landscape composition and configuration in biological invasions is widely considered while its interplay with landscape connectivity is less understood. However, ecological connectivity can be equally crucial for both native and alien species, constituting the backbone of ecological network initiatives. Objectives We aim to assess how landscape composition, configuration and connectivity (in the ecological network) influence α- and β-diversity (floristic uniqueness) of both alien and native plant species, and to determine whether these effects differ according to habitat type. Methods The study was conducted in a 298 km 2 ecological network in the lowlands of Friuli Venezia Giulia, northeastern Italy, encompassing a mosaic of agricultural, natural, and semi-natural habitats. A hierarchical sampling design was applied to 87 terrestrial habitat nodes, where plant species composition and abundance were recorded in 219 plots. Landscape composition, configuration and connectivity were quantified to examine their influence on native and alien plant α- and β-diversity across different habitat types. Results We found contrasting effects of landscape connectivity, composition and configuration for native and alien species. Peripheral, less connected sites favored native species richness (α-diversity) and contributed to maintaining native floristic uniqueness (high β-diversity). In contrast, alien species richness was mainly associated with landscape composition and configuration, particularly the proportion of natural land use and edge-related effects in wooded habitats, while plots with higher alien richness showed lower compositional uniqueness within the alien species pool. Landscape composition and configuration also influenced invasion dynamics, as nodes surrounded by a high proportion of natural land uses with simple shapes helped contain plant invasions while preserving native richness and uniqueness. These patterns were often habitat-dependent, with stronger effects observed in wooded areas, where alien α-diversity increased with fragmentation, whereas native species richness declined. Conclusions Our findings suggest that managing landscape connectivity and reducing fragmentation can enhance resistance to invasions and support native species richness. Peripheral nodes may act as native refugia, supporting high native richness and floristic uniqueness, while more accessible central nodes may function as alien hubs associated with greater alien compositional uniqueness and potential propagule exchange. Shifting from intensive to extensive land uses through green infrastructures provides a win–win strategy, promoting native species and limit alien establishment.

items.title: The science-policy gap on invasive species management: a review of research capacity, regulations, and data availability for an intergovernmental framework in the gulf cooperation council
items.abstract: Invasive alien species (IAS) pose major threats to biodiversity, ecosystem function, and agriculture, undermining progress on the Sustainable Development Goals. The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), with its arid climate, rapid urbanisation, dependence on imports, and ecologically fragile, endemic-rich habitats, is especially vulnerable. This paper constructs bridges over the science–policy gap in invasive species management through a systematic review of national and regional regulatory frameworks, global invasion ecology publications, and 3.9 million biodiversity records. GCC institutions contribute only 0.6% of global invasion-ecology publications and, when normalised by GDP, produce invasion science at less than one-third of the global rate. Across the GCC, only 84 of 707 GRIIS-listed IAS (11.9%) are regulated, despite significant economic impacts. Critical deficiencies include species-specific laws, pathway controls, enforcement, and cross-border coordination, as most nations address invasive species only within broader biodiversity strategies. To remedy this, we propose an Inter-Governmental Invasive Species Science-Policy Platform (IISSPP), modelled on the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES), a lean intergovernmental science–policy platform built around regular assessments, early warning and knowledge generation, policy support, and capacity building. IISSPP would harmonise regulations, standardise risk assessments, unify watch lists, and promote open data sharing. The IISSPP model is replicable in other rapidly developing regions and supports global biodiversity targets under the Kunming–Montreal Framework while advancing regional sustainable development and climate resilience.

items.title: Integrating land-use and climate connectivity to link protected areas at the country level
items.abstract: Context Ecological corridors that are high in biodiversity potential and stable under climate change are central to long-term conservation planning. The ensemble highlighted areas of high concordance across parameterizations, improving the robustness of spatial priorities. items.title: A standardized workflow for compiling and harmonizing first records of non-native species

items.title: Spatial and historical effects shape a wide‐scale rice field ostracod metacommunity pervaded by invasive species

To determine the processes that govern community assembly and biodiversity patterns, it is necessary to know the relative importance of these elements. In this study, we examine the ostracod metacommunity of rice fields across the Iberian Peninsula, aiming to assess the influence of spatial constraints, historical contingency (as derived from taphocoenoses remains), and environmental variables on the present metacommunity (biocoenoses) structure. We hypothesized that while all three components would affect the metacommunity, spatial effects would be particularly relevant due to the large geographical scope and associated dispersal limitations. Our results indicate that space was the most relevant factor in structuring the metacommunity, operating at broad and fine scales. Historical contingency also contributed substantially, as indicated by the high concordance between taphocoenoses and biocoenoses, suggesting that past community composition influences present assemblages, possibly through colonization advantages associated with egg banks. Although the pure environmental fraction was comparatively weak and nonsignificant, likely due to the low environmental variability of these homogeneous and artificially controlled aquatic habitats, the substantial shared environmental-spatial fraction could indicate that environmental conditions covaried with broad-scale spatial structure among regions. A notable number of invasive ostracods were identified, suggesting ongoing, albeit infrequent, colonization processes, probably facilitated by waterbirds, land ploughing, movement of agricultural machinery, and farmer activities, which support the establishment of invasive species within each community egg bank. These findings indicate that biodiversity management in seasonal agricultural landscapes, such as rice fields, should extend beyond local environmental conditions, taking into account regional connectivity, the persistence of egg-bank legacies, and human-mediated dispersal pathways that may facilitate the establishment of non-native species.

items.title: Resource subsidies mediated by non-native species: a review
items.abstract: NeoBiota 109: 315-343 DOI: 10.3897/neobiota.109.193175 Authors: Letícia Alves, Janeide Padilha, Phillip J. Haubrock, Amanda Subalusky, Ronaldo Sousa Abstract: Non-native species are recognized as one of the major drivers of biodiversity change globally, with profound impacts on ecosystem functions and services. Despite the high number of studies on non-native species published, mainly in the last two decades, an often-overlooked aspect is their role as mediators of resource subsidies (the cross-boundary movement of energy, nutrients, or materials). This topic may have theoretical and empirical implications because non-native species may play a major role in ecosystem connectivity by transporting—or interrupting the transport of—energy and organic matter. Therefore, the main aims of this review were to (1) assess temporal trends, geographic distribution, and methodological approaches in research on resource subsidies mediated by non-native species; (2) synthesize how non-native species alter the magnitude, direction, and dynamics of resource subsidies across ecosystems and their implications for ecosystem functioning; and (3) identify key gaps in current knowledge and define future research priorities. The review retrieved 143 publications, resulting in 212 case studies, that collectively show that non-native species can both reduce and increase resource flows across ecosystem boundaries, with implications for ecosystem dynamics and connectivity. Although terrestrial and freshwater connectivity accounted for the majority of published case studies (56%), many ecosystem linkages remain underexplored. A significant geographic bias was found, with Africa being severely understudied (2.8% of all publications), followed by Asia (7.7% of all publications). Taxonomic representation was also skewed, with the majority of studies focusing on non-native plants (28.8% of case studies), non-native fish (25.5% of case studies), and mammals (21.7% of case studies), whereas fungi (0.9%) and bacteria (2.4%) were largely neglected despite their fundamental roles in decomposition processes. Key priorities for advancing this field include long-term monitoring, the application of emerging molecular and analytical tools (e.g., telemetry, eDNA, metabarcoding, and isotopic tracers), and the integration of artificial intelligence to synthesize large datasets. The findings provide the first synthesis of resource subsidies mediated by non-native species. This information is crucial for biodiversity conservation and the effective management of ecosystems and their connectivity. HTML XML PDF

items.title: Effects of climate change on marine biodiversity on the western Atlantic coast
items.abstract: The current climate crisis, driven by greenhouse gas emissions, threatens global biodiversity, including that in marine ecosystems. However, projections for the western Atlantic Ocean that jointly quantify species richness and endemism while accounting for spatially biased and incomplete occurrence data remain limited. We addressed this gap across the western Atlantic from 57°S to 40°N, within 1500 km of the coast and on the continental shelf in waters shallower than 150 m. Using broad taxonomic coverage across vertebrates, invertebrates, and algae, we modeled biodiversity metrics directly as species richness and the corrected weighted endemism index (WEIc), applied uniform sampling from sampling effort (USSE) to minimize the effects of spatially biased and incomplete occurrence records on predictions, and tested multiple algorithms to project these metrics under Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 for 2050 and 2100. The results indicated a significant reduction in species richness and endemism, with up to 69% of the study area projected to experience a reduction of more than 5% in species richness under the high-emissions scenarios. The most affected areas included the coast of Florida, the Gulf of Mexico, the Caribbean, the northern region of South America, and southern Brazil. The decrease in endemism was equally concerning, with significant reductions predicted in areas of high diversity, threatening species adapted to specific ecological niches and increasing the risk of local extinctions. Vertebrates and invertebrates showed the greatest reductions in richness in the Gulf of Mexico, the Caribbean, northeastern Brazil, and northern Argentina. For algae, the most significant decreases were predicted for Florida and southern Brazil. This loss of biodiversity could compromise the resilience of marine ecosystems and the availability of fishery resources, highlighting the urgent need for coordinated global actions.

items.title: Legacy effects of land use land cover change on species distribution dynamics: evidence from a landscape of diverse biogeographic crossroads
items.abstract: Context Land use and land cover (LULC) change is a key driver of biodiversity distribution, yet species responses vary among taxa, habitats, and regions. Because species responses are context-dependent, understanding how ecological characteristics and landscape history influence biodiversity distribution is essential for conservation planning. Objectives We evaluated how nearly two centuries of LULC change have influenced vertebrate distribution dynamics across Texas, USA, a landscape of biogeographic crossroads. We tested whether habitat specialization, taxonomic identity, conservation status, and ecoregional context better explain range expansion, contraction, and redistribution than landscape change metrics alone. Methods We compared historical and contemporary distributions of 100 native vertebrate species (mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians). Multi-temporal LULC datasets (1850–2023) were integrated with species occurrences, habitat associations, and ecoregional data to identify drivers of distribution range change. Results LULC change was spatially heterogeneous, driven by agricultural expansion, cropland abandonment, shrubland encroachment, and urbanization. Most species shifted ranges, with responses varying by habitat, taxon, and ecoregion. Habitat specialists, reptiles, and amphibians showed the greatest contractions, whereas birds were comparably stable or expanding, with responses differing among ecoregions. Habitat affinity, vertebrate class, and ecoregional identity were stronger predictors of range change than landscape transformation metrics alone. Conclusions LULC legacies set the environmental template and influence species distributions indirectly through ecological filtering, species-specific traits, and regional context rather than change magnitude alone. By linking historical landscape trajectories with contemporary biodiversity patterns, this study provides a useful template for understanding land use legacies, species redistribution, and community reassembly in diverse landscapes, emphasizing adaptive capacity and connectivity for conservation planning.
